claim: Cytolysin is produced by many clinical isolates of Enterococcus faecalis.
source: Cytolysin is produced by many clinical isolates of Enterococcus faecalis and consists of two post-translationally modified peptides termed cytolysin L and S (Figure 1A) (Gilmore et al., 1994; Cox et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gilmore et al., 1994 and Cox et al., 2005

claim: Cytolysin consists of two post-translationally modified peptides termed cytolysin L and S.
source: Cytolysin is produced by many clinical isolates of Enterococcus faecalis and consists of two post-translationally modified peptides termed cytolysin L and S (Figure 1A) (Gilmore et al., 1994; Cox et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gilmore et al., 1994 and Cox et al., 2005, and illustrated in Figure 1A

claim: Cytolysin peptides have lytic activity against various types of eukaryotic cells including immune cells.
source: These peptides have lytic activity against various types of eukaryotic cells including immune cells (Cox et al., 2005; Bierbaum and Sahl, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cox et al., 2005 and Bierbaum and Sahl, 2009

claim: The production of cytolysin enhances virulence in infection models of E. faecalis.
source: The production of cytolysin enhances virulence in infection models of E. faecalis, and epidemiological data support an association with acute patient mortality (Ike and Clewell, 1984; Huycke et al., 1991; Chow et al., 1993; Van Tyne et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ike and Clewell, 1984; Huycke et al., 1991; Chow et al., 1993; Van Tyne et al., 2013

claim: Epidemiological data support an association between cytolysin production and acute patient mortality.
source: The production of cytolysin enhances virulence in infection models of E. faecalis, and epidemiological data support an association with acute patient mortality (Ike and Clewell, 1984; Huycke et al., 1991; Chow et al., 1993; Van Tyne et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ike and Clewell, 1984; Huycke et al., 1991; Chow et al., 1993; Van Tyne et al., 2013

claim: Cytolysin is a member of the lanthipeptides.
source: Cytolysin is a member of the lanthipeptides, a family of polycyclic peptides that are made in a two-step process involving dehydration of Ser and Thr residues to dehydroamino acids and subsequent addition of thiols of Cys residues to the dehydroamino acids (Figure 1B) (Knerr and van der Donk, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Knerr and van der Donk, 2012

claim: Lanthipeptides are a family of polycyclic peptides made in a two-step process involving dehydration of Ser and Thr residues to dehydroamino acids and subsequent addition of thiols of Cys residues to the dehydroamino acids.
source: Cytolysin is a member of the lanthipeptides, a family of polycyclic peptides that are made in a two-step process involving dehydration of Ser and Thr residues to dehydroamino acids and subsequent addition of thiols of Cys residues to the dehydroamino acids (Figure 1B) (Knerr and van der Donk, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Knerr and van der Donk, 2012 and illustrated in Figure 1B

claim: CylM catalyzes the dehydration and cyclization reactions during cytolysin biosynthesis.
source: This process, catalyzed by the enzyme CylM for cytolysin, generates the characteristic thioether crosslinks called lanthionine (Lan) and methyllanthionine (MeLan) (Figure 1).
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1

claim: The process catalyzed by CylM generates the characteristic thioether crosslinks called lanthionine (Lan) and methyllanthionine (MeLan).
source: This process, catalyzed by the enzyme CylM for cytolysin, generates the characteristic thioether crosslinks called lanthionine (Lan) and methyllanthionine (MeLan) (Figure 1).
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1

claim: An N-terminal leader peptide in the substrates is important for substrate binding by lanthipeptide biosynthetic enzymes.
source: An N-terminal leader peptide in the substrates is important for substrate binding by lanthipeptide biosynthetic enzymes (Oman and van der Donk, 2010), but the post-translational modifications take place in the C-terminal core peptides.
evidence: Supported by citation to Oman and van der Donk, 2010

claim: Post-translational modifications in lanthipeptides take place in the C-terminal core peptides.
source: An N-terminal leader peptide in the substrates is important for substrate binding by lanthipeptide biosynthetic enzymes (Oman and van der Donk, 2010), but the post-translational modifications take place in the C-terminal core peptides.
evidence: Stated in text as established knowledge

claim: Four distinct routes to lanthipeptides have been discovered.
source: To date, four distinct routes to lanthipeptides have been discovered, illustrating that the cyclic thioether motif is a privileged structural scaffold that has been independently accessed multiple times during evolution (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2012

claim: The cyclic thioether motif is a privileged structural scaffold that has been independently accessed multiple times during evolution.
source: To date, four distinct routes to lanthipeptides have been discovered, illustrating that the cyclic thioether motif is a privileged structural scaffold that has been independently accessed multiple times during evolution (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2012 and inference from the discovery of four distinct routes

claim: The thioether bridges introduce conformational constraints that facilitate target binding and reduce proteolytic susceptibility.
source: The thioether bridges introduce conformational constraints that facilitate target binding and reduce proteolytic susceptibility.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about lanthipeptide structure-function relationships

claim: The four routes to lanthipeptides differ primarily in the mechanism of dehydration.
source: The four routes differ primarily in the mechanism of dehydration.
evidence: Stated as a summary of differences between lanthipeptide biosynthetic pathways

claim: For class I, III, and IV lanthipeptides, the mechanism of dehydration has been illuminated by crystallographic characterization of the dehydratases or close sequence homologs.
source: For the class I, III, and IV lanthipeptides, the mechanism of dehydration has been illuminated by crystallographic characterization of the dehydratases or close sequence homologs (Li et al., 2006, 2007; Goto et al., 2010; Ortega et al., 2015), but the mechanism of dehydration for class II lanthipeptide synthetases (LanMs) that include CylM has remained enigmatic.
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2006, 2007; Goto et al., 2010; Ortega et al., 2015

claim: The mechanism of dehydration for class II lanthipeptide synthetases (LanMs) that include CylM has remained enigmatic.
source: For the class I, III, and IV lanthipeptides, the mechanism of dehydration has been illuminated by crystallographic characterization of the dehydratases or close sequence homologs (Li et al., 2006, 2007; Goto et al., 2010; Ortega et al., 2015), but the mechanism of dehydration for class II lanthipeptide synthetases (LanMs) that include CylM has remained enigmatic.
evidence: Stated as the knowledge gap that this study addresses

claim: Class II lanthipeptide synthetases show no clear sequence homology with non-lanthipeptide proteins.
source: These enzymes show no clear sequence homology with non-lanthipeptide proteins and despite two decades of investigation, structural information on class II lanthipeptide synthetases has been unavailable.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about LanM enzymes

claim: Despite two decades of investigation, structural information on class II lanthipeptide synthetases has been unavailable prior to this study.
source: These enzymes show no clear sequence homology with non-lanthipeptide proteins and despite two decades of investigation, structural information on class II lanthipeptide synthetases has been unavailable.
evidence: Stated as the knowledge gap that this study addresses

claim: Structural information on LanM enzymes would be valuable for obtaining inhibitors of cytolysin biosynthesis that could be therapeutically valuable.
source: Such information would be valuable for obtaining inhibitors of cytolysin biosynthesis that could be therapeutically valuable.
evidence: Stated as speculation about the potential applications of structural information

claim: LanM lanthipeptide synthetases are involved in the biosynthesis of several lanthipeptides and their derivatives that are under clinical evaluation such as actagardine and duramycin.
source: In addition, LanM lanthipeptide synthetases are involved in the biosynthesis of several lanthipeptides and their derivatives that are under clinical evaluation such as actagardine and duramycin (Grasemann et al., 2007; Steiner et al., 2008; Jones and Helm, 2009; Johnson, 2010; Oliynyk et al., 2010; Crowther et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grasemann et al., 2007; Steiner et al., 2008; Jones and Helm, 2009; Johnson, 2010; Oliynyk et al., 2010; Crowther et al., 2013

claim: Structural information on LanM synthetases will facilitate bioengineering of improved analogs.
source: As such, structural information on this class of synthetases will also facilitate bioengineering of improved analogs.
evidence: Stated as speculation about the potential applications of structural information

claim: The 2.2 Å resolution structure of CylM was determined.
source: We describe here the 2.2 Å resolution structure of CylM and demonstrate that its dehydration domain surprisingly has structural similarity with eukaryotic lipid kinases despite the absence of notable sequence homology.
evidence: Reported as the main experimental result of this study

claim: The dehydration domain of CylM has structural similarity with eukaryotic lipid kinases despite the absence of notable sequence homology.
source: We describe here the 2.2 Å resolution structure of CylM and demonstrate that its dehydration domain surprisingly has structural similarity with eukaryotic lipid kinases despite the absence of notable sequence homology.
evidence: Reported as the main finding from structural analysis

claim: One eukaryotic homolog of lanthipeptide cyclases was recently shown to interact with mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) complex 2.
source: These findings may also have implications for the three eukaryotic homologs of lanthipeptide cyclases, one of which was recently shown to interact with mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) complex 2 (Zeng et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zeng et al., 2014

claim: There are three eukaryotic homologs of lanthipeptide cyclases.
source: These findings may also have implications for the three eukaryotic homologs of lanthipeptide cyclases, one of which was recently shown to interact with mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) complex 2 (Zeng et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: CylM and its substrate peptides CylLL and CylLS were expressed in Escherichia coli as hexahistidine-tagged proteins.
source: CylM and its substrate peptides CylLL and CylLS were expressed in Escherichia coli as hexahistidine-tagged proteins and purified by metal affinity chromatography.
evidence: Described as the experimental method used in this study

claim: Incubation of CylM with CylLL or CylLS in the presence of MgCl2 and ATP resulted in the desired number of dehydrations.
source: Incubation of CylM with CylLL or CylLS in the presence of MgCl2 and adenosine triphosphate (ATP), and subsequent removal of the leader peptides by purified CylA, a serine protease of the cytolysin biosynthetic pathway (Booth et al., 1996), resulted in the desired number of dehydrations as determined by matrix-assisted laser-desorption time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: CylA is a serine protease of the cytolysin biosynthetic pathway.
source: Incubation of CylM with CylLL or CylLS in the presence of MgCl2 and adenosine triphosphate (ATP), and subsequent removal of the leader peptides by purified CylA, a serine protease of the cytolysin biosynthetic pathway (Booth et al., 1996), resulted in the desired number of dehydrations as determined by matrix-assisted laser-desorption time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Booth et al., 1996

claim: Analysis of the peptides by tandem ESI MS demonstrated the formation of the correct ring structures.
source: Analysis of the peptides by tandem electrospray ionization mass spectrometry (ESI MS) demonstrated the formation of the correct ring structures (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The structure of the ∼110 kDa CylM polypeptide consists of two distinct domains.
source: The structure of the ∼110 kDa polypeptide consists of two distinct domains, with an N-terminal dehydration domain, composed of residues Asn4 through Pro624, and a C-terminal cyclization domain encompassed by Tyr641 through Glu992 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Reported from structural analysis and shown in Figure 2A

claim: CylM has an N-terminal dehydration domain composed of residues Asn4 through Pro624.
source: The structure of the ∼110 kDa polypeptide consists of two distinct domains, with an N-terminal dehydration domain, composed of residues Asn4 through Pro624, and a C-terminal cyclization domain encompassed by Tyr641 through Glu992 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Reported from structural analysis and shown in Figure 2A

claim: CylM has a C-terminal cyclization domain encompassed by Tyr641 through Glu992.
source: The structure of the ∼110 kDa polypeptide consists of two distinct domains, with an N-terminal dehydration domain, composed of residues Asn4 through Pro624, and a C-terminal cyclization domain encompassed by Tyr641 through Glu992 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Reported from structural analysis and shown in Figure 2A

claim: CylM is a monomer in the crystal and in solution as determined by gel filtration analysis.
source: The protein is a monomer in the crystal and in solution as determined by gel filtration analysis.
evidence: Reported from experimental gel filtration analysis

claim: The cyclization domain of CylM consists of the α/α-barrel fold observed in the structure of the stand-alone class I Lan cyclase NisC.
source: Consistent with prior predictions, the cyclization domain consists of the α/α-barrel fold observed in the structure of the stand-alone class I Lan cyclase NisC (Li et al., 2006).
evidence: Reported from structural comparison and supported by citation to Li et al., 2006

claim: CylM contains a single zinc ion near the center of the toroid coordinated by residues Cys875, Cys911, and His912, with a water molecule completing the tetrahedral coordination geometry at the metal.
source: As in NisC, CylM contains a single zinc ion near the center of the toroid coordinated by residues Cys875, Cys911, and His912, with a water molecule completing the tetrahedral coordination geometry at the metal.

claim: The zinc site in CylM is believed to activate the thiols of the Cys residues during the cyclization reaction.
source: This zinc site is believed to activate the thiols of the Cys residues during the cyclization reaction (Li et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2006 and inference from structural similarity to NisC

claim: The barrel of the NisC structure is interspersed with a structural element that resembles eukaryotic peptide-binding domains.
source: The barrel of the NisC structure is interspersed with a structural element that resembles eukaryotic peptide-binding domains (Figure 2B), which is thought to bind the leader region of the substrate peptide.
evidence: Reported from structural analysis and shown in Figure 2B

claim: The structural element in NisC is thought to bind the leader region of the substrate peptide.
source: The barrel of the NisC structure is interspersed with a structural element that resembles eukaryotic peptide-binding domains (Figure 2B), which is thought to bind the leader region of the substrate peptide.
evidence: Stated as inference from structural features

claim: The C-terminal cyclization domain of CylM lacks the peptide-binding element found in NisC but instead contains a β-sheet region composed of three antiparallel strands that is situated near the zinc ion.
source: The C-terminal cyclization domain of CylM lacks this element but instead contains a β-sheet region composed of three antiparallel strands that is situated near the zinc ion (Figure 2A, red).
evidence: Reported from structural analysis and shown in Figure 2A

claim: The β-sheet element in CylM, encompassing Ile666 through Leu690, is located on the opposite face of the toroid relative to the putative leader peptide-binding domain in NisC.
source: This element, encompassing Ile666 through Leu690, is located on the opposite face of the toroid relative to the putative leader peptide-binding domain in NisC, where it flanks against the base of the N-terminal dehydration domain of CylM.
evidence: Reported from structural analysis

claim: A similar antiparallel β-stranded element engages the leader peptide in the mechanistically unrelated class I Lan dehydratase NisB.
source: A similar antiparallel β-stranded element engages the leader peptide in the mechanistically unrelated class I Lan dehydratase NisB (Ortega et al., 2015) and is also found in other enzymes involved in the biosynthesis of ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs) (Koehnke et al., 2013; Burkhart et al., 2015; Koehnke et al., 2015) (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ortega et al., 2015; Koehnke et al., 2013; Burkhart et al., 2015; Koehnke et al., 2015 and shown in Figure 2C

claim: The leader peptide binding architecture may be conserved across RiPP biosynthetic enzymes, despite very high diversity of the reactions they catalyze.
source: Thus, the leader peptide binding architecture may be conserved across RiPP biosynthetic enzymes, despite very high diversity of the reactions they catalyze (Arnison et al., 2013).
evidence: Inferred from structural comparisons and supported by citation to Arnison et al., 2013

claim: The N-terminal domain of CylM (residues 1–625) that lacks the β-stranded element resulted in efficient dehydration when incubated with CylLS substrate.
source: To investigate whether the β-stranded element in the cyclase domain is important for the dehydration reaction, the N-terminal domain (residues 1–625) that lacks this element was expressed and purified with an N-terminal His6-tag. Incubation with CylLS substrate resulted in efficient dehydration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that the β-stranded element is not required for the dehydration reaction.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The β-stranded element is not required for the dehydration reaction.
source: Incubation with CylLS substrate resulted in efficient dehydration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that the β-stranded element is not required for the dehydration reaction.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Recent reports describe expression and activity of the two individual domains of various LanM enzymes and binding of their substrates to both domains.
source: This observation is consistent with several very recent reports describing expression and activity of the two individual domains of various LanM enzymes and binding of their substrates to both domains (Ma et al., 2015; Shimafuji et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ma et al., 2015; Shimafuji et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2015

claim: The N-terminal dehydration domain of CylM lacks detectable sequence similarities with other proteins.
source: Although the N-terminal dehydration domain lacks detectable sequence similarities with other proteins, the CylM structure reveals that this domain is architecturally related to the catalytic core of lipid kinases, such as phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) (Figure 2A,D) (Walker et al., 1999; Williams et al., 2009).
evidence: Stated as observation from sequence analysis

claim: The CylM dehydration domain is architecturally related to the catalytic core of lipid kinases, such as phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K).
source: Although the N-terminal dehydration domain lacks detectable sequence similarities with other proteins, the CylM structure reveals that this domain is architecturally related to the catalytic core of lipid kinases, such as phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) (Figure 2A,D) (Walker et al., 1999; Williams et al., 2009).
evidence: Reported from structural analysis, shown in Figure 2A,D, and supported by citations to Walker et al., 1999; Williams et al., 2009

claim: The structural similarity of CylM with kinases is consistent with the proposed mechanism of dehydration by LanM proteins via first phosphorylation of Ser and Thr residues, followed by elimination of the phosphate.
source: The structural similarity with kinases is consistent with the proposed mechanism of dehydration by LanM proteins via first phosphorylation of Ser and Thr residues, followed by elimination of the phosphate (Chatterjee et al., 2005; You and van der Donk, 2007).
evidence: Inferred from structural similarity and supported by citations to Chatterjee et al., 2005; You and van der Donk, 2007

claim: The topology of the CylM dehydration domain is quite different from those of canonical kinases.
source: Despite the structural homology, the topology of the CylM dehydration domain is quite different from those of canonical kinases (Figure 2E), resulting in a distinct connectivity between conserved secondary structural features (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), which can only be gleaned through a structure-based alignment (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Reported from structural analysis and shown in Figures 2E, 2—figure supplement 2, and 2—figure supplement 3

claim: The CylM dehydration domain is composed of an N-lobe spanning residues Lys135 through Ser279, and a C-lobe composed of residues Glu280 through Val508.
source: Like canonical kinases, the CylM dehydration domain is composed of an N-lobe spanning residues Lys135 through Ser279, and a C-lobe composed of residues Glu280 through Val508 (Figure 3A).

claim: A number of helices formed by residues Leu5 through Asn131 and a two-helix insert created by Ile180 through Tyr200 cap the N-lobe of CylM.

claim: A similar, but topologically distinct, four-helix bundle insertion (termed the FRB domain) cradles the N-lobe of PI3K-related protein kinases (PIKKs) such as mTOR and DNA-PKc.
source: A similar, but topologically distinct, four-helix bundle insertion (termed the FRB domain [Chen et al., 1995]) cradles the N-lobe of PI3K-related protein kinases (PIKKs) such as, mTOR and DNA-PKc (Figure 3B,C) (Choi et al., 1996; Sibanda et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: Reported from structural comparison and supported by citations to Chen et al., 1995; Choi et al., 1996; Sibanda et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2013

claim: The CylM C-lobe is appended with two helices formed by Gln589 through Pro624 that are characteristic of lipid kinases (helices kα10 and kα11 in lipid kinase nomenclature).
source: The CylM C-lobe is appended with two helices formed by Gln589 through Pro624 that are characteristic of lipid kinases (helices kα10 and kα11 in lipid kinase nomenclature) (Walker et al., 1999; Miller et al., 2010; Sibanda et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: Reported from structural analysis and supported by citations to Walker et al., 1999; Miller et al., 2010; Sibanda et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2013

claim: Helix kα11 of CylM packs against the three-β-stranded proposed leader peptide-binding region in the cyclase domain.
source: Helix kα11 of CylM packs against the three-β-stranded proposed leader peptide-binding region in the cyclase domain (Figure 3A).
evidence: Reported from structural analysis and shown in Figure 3A

claim: In mTOR, the equivalent kα11 helix is necessary for stabilization of the activation loop.
source: In mTOR, the equivalent kα11 helix is necessary for stabilization of the activation loop (Figure 3B) (Yang et al., 2013).

claim: The CylM dehydration domain is considerably larger than the catalytic domain of other protein and lipid kinases, with the exception of PIKKs that contain the FRB insertion within the N-lobe.

claim: All protein and lipid kinases contain a requisite ∼30-residue segment termed the activation loop that plays a major role in both regulation and function.
source: All protein and lipid kinases contain a requisite ∼30-residue segment termed the activation loop that plays a major role in both regulation and function.

claim: Kinase activity is typically controlled through activation-induced conformational changes, consisting of a disorder-to-order transition of the activation loop.

claim: Unlike most kinases, the activation loop in the CylM dehydration domain, composed of residues Asn365 through Val383, is well defined in the absence of bound peptide substrate.
source: Unlike most kinases, the activation loop in the CylM dehydration domain, composed of residues Asn365 through Val383, is well defined in the absence of bound peptide substrate (Figures 2A, 3A).

claim: The orientation and stabilization of the activation loop in CylM is established through numerous interactions with the LanM-specific KA domain.

claim: The activation loop in CylM is presumably stabilized in a catalytically competent conformation, because unlike most lipid kinases, the dehydration activity of LanM enzymes is not dependent on exogenous regulatory protein activators.
source: The activation loop is presumably stabilized in a catalytically competent conformation, because unlike most lipid kinases, the dehydration activity of LanM enzymes is not dependent on exogenous regulatory protein activators.

claim: The activation loop in mTOR is similarly held in a catalytically competent conformation via interactions with a highly conserved and integral ∼35 residue FATC domain, which is stabilized through packing interactions with a ∼40 residue insertion in the C-lobe termed the LBE.

claim: In the CylM co-crystal structure, the bound AMP is located between the two lobes of the kinase domain.

claim: The phosphate-binding loop (P-loop) in CylM is composed of residues Ser247 through Thr262 and is considerably longer than the equivalent feature in PI3Ks.

claim: The P-loop in CylM contains many residues that are poised to interact with the nucleotide phosphate, including Asp252 and His254.
